title: Diabetes: Diagnose, Confirm, Classify
bottomLine: Use Canadian diagnostic thresholds correctly, confirm an abnormal result in an asymptomatic patient, and do not let the label 'type 2' delay insulin when the presentation suggests insulin deficiency or metabolic decompensation.
recognize: Diabetes Canada diagnostic thresholds include fasting plasma glucose at or above 7.0 mmol/L, A1C at or above 6.5% in appropriate adults, 2-hour 75 g OGTT plasma glucose at or above 11.1 mmol/L, or random plasma glucose at or above 11.1 mmol/L.
In symptomatic hyperglycemia, one diagnostic-range result is sufficient; without symptoms, a single abnormal laboratory result requires timely confirmation.
Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, blurred vision, recurrent infections or ketosis increase urgency.
differentiate: A1C is unreliable in some hemoglobinopathies, altered red-cell turnover, significant anemia, severe renal/hepatic disease and certain other conditions; use glucose-based criteria when accuracy is doubtful.
Lean body habitus, rapid weight loss, ketosis, autoimmune history or rapid deterioration can suggest type 1/LADA rather than routine type 2 diabetes.
assessment: Assess symptoms, weight trajectory, pregnancy status, family history, medications such as glucocorticoids/antipsychotics and signs of insulin deficiency.
At diagnosis, assess BP, cardiovascular and renal risk, smoking, foot/neuropathy symptoms and access to nutrition/medications.
workup: Use FPG and/or A1C for routine screening; Diabetes Canada recommends screening at least every 3 years beginning at age 40 or earlier/more often with high risk.
Use ketones, electrolytes and acid-base evaluation urgently when metabolic decompensation is possible.
management: Begin education, nutrition/physical-activity support and individualized pharmacotherapy after classification and risk assessment.
Do not wait for outpatient confirmation when the patient has symptomatic severe hyperglycemia or suspected DKA/HHS.
medicationSafety: Before choosing therapy, review renal function, hypoglycemia risk, pregnancy, weight goals, cardiovascular/renal comorbidity and medication affordability.
redFlags: Marked dehydration or altered mental status
Unintentional weight loss with severe hyperglycemia
Vomiting or abdominal pain with SGLT2 inhibitor use
counselling: Explain that diabetes diagnosis is not based on symptoms alone and that treatment targets are individualized.
Use culturally appropriate, non-stigmatizing nutrition counselling rather than assigning blame for the diagnosis.
followUp: Arrange timely review of glycemia, medication tolerance and baseline complication screening after diagnosis.
examTrap: Repeating diagnostic testing before treating a symptomatic patient with severe hyperglycemia or ketosis because 'two tests are required'.
oneLinePearl: Confirm asymptomatic diabetes; treat symptomatic metabolic decompensation now.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Clinical Practice Guideline: Definition, Classification and Diagnosis

title: Type 2 Diabetes: Choose Therapy by Risk
bottomLine: Metformin remains the initial glucose-lowering medication for most adults who need pharmacotherapy, but cardiorenal disease changes the algorithm: use evidence-based SGLT2 inhibitors and/or GLP-1 receptor agonists for cardiovascular/renal protection when indicated even if A1C is already at target.
recognize: An A1C more than about 1.5 percentage points above the individualized target often requires initial combination therapy rather than slow monotherapy escalation.
Metabolic decompensation or severe symptomatic hyperglycemia is an insulin problem first, regardless of the A1C number.
Heart failure, CKD and high cardiovascular risk influence drug selection independently of glucose lowering.
differentiate: The best drug for lowering A1C is not always the best drug for the patient's cardiovascular/renal outcome.
Older/frail patients with recurrent hypoglycemia often benefit from de-intensification rather than pursuit of a lower A1C.
assessment: Set an individualized glycemic target based on age, function, comorbidity, hypoglycemia risk, life expectancy and patient priorities.
Assess eGFR, cardiovascular disease, HF, albuminuria/CKD, weight goals, hypoglycemia risk, cost/coverage and injection preference.
workup: Use A1C and glucose monitoring appropriate to the medication regimen; screen complications and cardiovascular risk factors.
Do not use A1C alone when factors make it unreliable.
management: Start metformin for most people requiring pharmacotherapy unless contraindicated/not tolerated.
Use insulin promptly for metabolic decompensation/severe symptomatic hyperglycemia.
Add specific GLP-1RA and/or SGLT2 inhibitors for cardiorenal protection when high CV risk, HF or CKD warrants them, even if A1C is controlled.
Select additional agents based on hypoglycemia, weight, renal function, adverse effects, cost and patient preference.
medicationSafety: SGLT2 inhibitors carry a rare euglycemic DKA risk: hold during major surgery, severe acute illness, significant fasting or volume depletion according to sick-day/perioperative guidance.
Avoid combining a GLP-1RA with a DPP-4 inhibitor for routine glycemic management.
Sulfonylureas and insulin have higher hypoglycemia risk, especially with CKD, irregular food intake or frailty.
redFlags: Ketosis, severe dehydration or symptomatic marked hyperglycemia
Possible euglycemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitor
counselling: Explain why a medication may be used for heart/kidney protection even when glucose looks 'good'.
Review sick-day rules and hypoglycemia prevention for relevant therapies.
followUp: Reassess A1C, symptoms, hypoglycemia, weight, renal function and medication tolerance after changes; intensify or de-intensify based on goals.
examTrap: Refusing an SGLT2 inhibitor/GLP-1RA because the A1C is already at target despite a clear cardiorenal indication—or delaying insulin in metabolic decompensation.
oneLinePearl: Treat glucose, but choose drugs for the heart and kidneys too.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Pharmacologic Glycemic Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Adults 2024 Update

title: Hypoglycemia: Treat, Prevent the Repeat
bottomLine: Correct hypoglycemia immediately, then identify why it happened. A recurrent low is a medication-safety event until proven otherwise, especially with insulin, sulfonylureas, CKD, frailty, food insecurity or hypoglycemia unawareness.
recognize: Autonomic symptoms include tremor, sweating, palpitations and hunger; neuroglycopenic symptoms include confusion, behaviour change, visual disturbance, seizure and loss of consciousness.
Older adults may present with falls, delirium or weakness rather than classic adrenergic symptoms.
differentiate: A conscious patient who can swallow can use oral fast-acting carbohydrate; an unconscious or unsafe-swallow patient requires glucagon or IV dextrose and emergency support.
Sulfonylurea-related hypoglycemia can recur after initial correction.
assessment: Check glucose promptly; assess level of consciousness, airway protection and seizure/injury.
Review insulin timing/dose, missed meals, exercise, alcohol, renal function, medication changes and access to food.
workup: After stabilization, investigate recurrent/unexplained episodes based on medication exposure, renal/hepatic disease, infection, adrenal disease or other clinical clues.
management: For a conscious adult able to swallow, use rapidly absorbed carbohydrate and recheck glucose after treatment according to the Diabetes Canada protocol.
For level-3 hypoglycemia with inability to swallow, use glucagon when IV access is unavailable or IV dextrose when available; activate emergency services as appropriate.
After recovery, provide longer-acting carbohydrate/meal as needed and adjust the precipitating medication/behaviour.
medicationSafety: Recurrent hypoglycemia should trigger de-intensification or regimen redesign rather than simply telling the patient to 'eat more'.
Prescribe/teach glucagon to high-risk patients and support persons when appropriate.
redFlags: Hypoglycemia in pregnancy or a patient living alone with impaired awareness
counselling: Teach recognition, carrying fast carbohydrate, driving safety and glucagon use where indicated.
Address food insecurity directly if meals are unreliable.
followUp: Any severe episode needs prompt medication review and prevention plan; consider technology/CGM and diabetes team support when appropriate.
examTrap: Treating the low successfully and discharging without changing the insulin/sulfonylurea regimen that caused it.
oneLinePearl: Fix the glucose, then fix the reason it fell.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Hypoglycemia in Adults 2023 Update

title: DKA and HHS: Fluids, Potassium, Insulin, Cause
bottomLine: DKA/HHS are emergencies. Think in parallel: restore volume, evaluate potassium, give insulin safely, monitor electrolytes/osmolality, and find the precipitating cause. DKA can occur with only modest glucose, especially with SGLT2 inhibitors.
recognize: DKA: ketosis and metabolic acidosis with dehydration; glucose may be high but euglycemic DKA exists.
HHS: profound hyperosmolar dehydration and hyperglycemia with less prominent ketosis/acidosis; altered mental status is common.
Common triggers include infection, missed insulin, new diabetes, MI/stroke, medications and acute illness.
differentiate: Vomiting can partially mask DKA acidosis by raising bicarbonate; use ketones/anion gap/acid-base data together.
Urine ketone tests can underestimate beta-hydroxybutyrate-predominant DKA; blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is more informative where available.
assessment: Assess ABCs, mental status, perfusion, volume depletion, infection/ischemia symptoms and medication history including SGLT2 inhibitors.
Obtain ECG when potassium disturbance is likely.
workup: Glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, venous/arterial acid-base testing as appropriate, beta-hydroxybutyrate/ketones, calculated anion gap and osmolality for HHS context.
Investigate precipitant with targeted cultures, ECG/troponin or imaging based on presentation.
management: Emergency/hospital management: isotonic fluid resuscitation, potassium-guided replacement, insulin and frequent biochemical monitoring.
Do not start insulin blindly in severe hypokalemia; potassium must be addressed because insulin shifts potassium intracellularly.
Continue treatment until ketoacidosis/hyperosmolality resolves clinically and biochemically, not merely until glucose normalizes.
medicationSafety: SGLT2 inhibitor-associated DKA may have glucose below the level expected for classic DKA.
Rapid osmotic shifts can cause neurologic harm; HHS correction requires careful monitoring.
counselling: After recovery, teach sick-day management, ketone testing where appropriate, insulin continuity and when to hold SGLT2 inhibitors.
followUp: Ensure the precipitating cause and access/adherence barriers are addressed before discharge; arrange prompt diabetes follow-up.
examTrap: Stopping treatment because the glucose normalized while the anion-gap acidosis/ketosis persists—or missing euglycemic DKA because glucose is not extremely high.
oneLinePearl: DKA is a ketone/acidosis emergency, not just a high-glucose emergency.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Hyperglycemic Emergencies in Adults

title: Thyroid Dysfunction: TSH-Centred Reasoning
bottomLine: For suspected primary thyroid dysfunction, start with TSH and add free T4 when the TSH is abnormal or when pituitary/hypothalamic disease makes TSH unreliable. Do not order broad thyroid panels reflexively.
recognize: Hypothyroidism: fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, menstrual change; symptoms are nonspecific.
Hyperthyroidism: heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, palpitations, anxiety, frequent stool, proximal weakness; older adults can present more subtly.
Thyroid storm and myxedema coma are rare emergencies with systemic decompensation, not merely abnormal TSH values.
differentiate: High TSH plus low free T4 supports primary hypothyroidism; suppressed TSH plus elevated free hormone supports primary hyperthyroidism.
Central hypothyroidism can have low free T4 with an inappropriately normal/low TSH—this is a situation where TSH alone fails.
Biotin and other assay interferences/acute illness can distort results.
assessment: Review pregnancy status, amiodarone/lithium, thyroid medication adherence/timing, neck symptoms, eye findings, AF, osteoporosis risk and pituitary symptoms.
workup: Use TSH as the first-line test in most suspected primary disease; add free T4 appropriately.
Do not routinely order free T3/free T4 panels or thyroid antibodies without a clinical question; target imaging/antibody testing to suspected etiology.
management: Treat overt primary hypothyroidism with levothyroxine, individualizing starting dose in older adults/coronary disease and separating administration from interfering medications/supplements.
Hyperthyroidism management depends on cause, severity and pregnancy; symptomatic beta-blockade and specialty-directed antithyroid therapy are common components.
Emergency decompensation requires acute-care treatment.
medicationSafety: Excess levothyroxine can cause AF and bone loss; titrate to TSH in primary hypothyroidism rather than symptoms alone.
Antithyroid drugs require counselling about rare serious adverse effects such as agranulocytosis/hepatotoxicity and pregnancy-specific selection.
redFlags: Hyperthermia, severe tachyarrhythmia, delirium or HF suggesting thyroid storm
Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation or coma suggesting myxedema coma
counselling: Explain that nonspecific symptoms can persist for reasons unrelated to thyroid hormone when TSH is appropriately controlled.
Review how calcium/iron and other agents can impair levothyroxine absorption.
followUp: Repeat TSH after an appropriate steady-state interval following levothyroxine dose changes; monitor more closely in pregnancy and major clinical change.
examTrap: Ordering T3, free T3, free T4 and antibody panels as the first test for every patient with fatigue—or adjusting levothyroxine based on free T4/T3 in uncomplicated primary hypothyroidism despite an appropriate TSH.
oneLinePearl: Primary thyroid disease is usually a TSH-first problem; central disease is the exception.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada / Canadian Society of Endocrinology and Metabolism Thyroid Testing Recommendations

title: Sodium and Potassium Emergencies
bottomLine: Electrolyte questions are urgency questions. Severe neurologic symptoms drive immediate hyponatremia care; ECG toxicity drives immediate hyperkalemia care. Correct the dangerous physiology while simultaneously identifying volume status, medication causes and the underlying disorder.
recognize: Hyponatremia can cause headache, confusion, vomiting, seizure and coma; chronic mild hyponatremia may cause gait/cognitive problems.
Hyperkalemia can cause weakness, paresthesia, bradyarrhythmia, conduction delay and malignant ventricular rhythms, but ECG can be deceptively normal.
Hypokalemia can cause weakness, ileus, arrhythmia and potentiation of digoxin toxicity.
differentiate: For hyponatremia, first confirm hypotonicity and assess volume status; hyperglycemia and pseudohyponatremia require different reasoning.
Urine osmolality and urine sodium help distinguish impaired water excretion/SIADH from hypovolemic and other causes.
A hemolyzed potassium specimen can cause pseudohyperkalemia—repeat if the clinical context and ECG do not fit, but never delay emergency treatment when toxicity is present.
assessment: Assess symptoms, acuity, fluid status, kidney function and medications: diuretics, ACEi/ARB/MRA, NSAIDs, SSRIs, carbamazepine, laxatives and supplements.
Obtain ECG promptly for significant potassium abnormalities.
workup: Use serum osmolality, urine osmolality/sodium, glucose, renal function and endocrine testing when indicated for hyponatremia.
For potassium disorders, assess magnesium, acid-base status, renal function and medication causes.
management: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia requires monitored hypertonic-saline management with controlled correction to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Hyperkalemia with ECG changes/severe level requires membrane stabilization, intracellular shift and definitive potassium removal in acute care.
Replace potassium/magnesium safely in hypokalemia while treating ongoing losses.
medicationSafety: Over-rapid sodium correction can cause osmotic demyelination; chronicity and risk factors matter.
RAAS inhibitors, MRAs, trimethoprim and potassium supplements can combine to produce dangerous hyperkalemia, especially in CKD.
counselling: Review fluid advice only after the cause is known; generic 'drink more water' can worsen hyponatremia.
Teach high-risk patients which medications/supplements contain potassium.
followUp: Repeat electrolytes at a clinically appropriate interval after correction or medication change; persistent unexplained abnormalities require etiologic workup.
examTrap: Giving free water to every low-sodium patient—or waiting for ECG changes before taking severe hyperkalemia seriously.
oneLinePearl: Symptoms set sodium urgency; ECG/toxicity sets potassium urgency.

title: Acute Kidney Injury: Pre-Renal, Intrinsic, Post-Renal
bottomLine: AKI management is cause-first: assess perfusion, nephrotoxins and obstruction immediately, treat life-threatening electrolyte/volume complications, and trend kidney function rather than reacting to creatinine in isolation.
recognize: Pre-renal: volume loss, sepsis, reduced effective circulating volume or hemodynamic medication effects.
Intrinsic: glomerular, tubular, interstitial or vascular injury; urinalysis and clinical context help.
Post-renal: retention, stones, prostate/urothelial obstruction or pelvic mass; bilateral obstruction/single kidney can rapidly cause AKI.
differentiate: A small creatinine rise can be clinically important; oliguria can precede a large creatinine change.
Not every ACEi/ARB-associated creatinine increase represents structural injury, but significant change requires volume/renal artery/medication assessment.
assessment: Assess volume status, BP/perfusion, urine output, recent illness, contrast/procedures and all nephrotoxins including OTC NSAIDs.
Ask about retention, flank pain, hematuria, systemic rash/fever and glomerular symptoms.
workup: Repeat creatinine/electrolytes, urinalysis with microscopy when useful, CBC and cause-directed tests.
Use bladder scan/renal ultrasound when obstruction is plausible; avoid indiscriminate imaging otherwise.
management: Restore perfusion if volume depleted while avoiding fluid overload.
Stop/hold nephrotoxins and renally adjust medication dosing.
Relieve obstruction promptly.
Escalate for refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, pulmonary edema, uremic complications or rapidly progressive/uncertain intrinsic renal disease.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs can worsen renal perfusion, especially with CKD, HF, dehydration or concurrent RAAS blockade/diuretics.
Review metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, anticoagulants and renally cleared drugs during significant AKI rather than continuing automatically.
redFlags: Rapidly rising creatinine with active urine sediment
counselling: Explain sick-day medication planning for patients at recurrent dehydration/AKI risk using local evidence-based instructions rather than blanket permanent discontinuation.
followUp: Recheck renal function after AKI, restore indicated chronic medications when safe and assess for residual CKD.
examTrap: Calling all AKI 'dehydration' and giving fluids without checking for pulmonary congestion or obstruction.
oneLinePearl: In AKI: perfusion, poison, plumbing—check all three.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Nephrology Practice Resources

title: CKD: eGFR Plus Albuminuria
bottomLine: CKD risk is not captured by eGFR alone. Combine persistent eGFR reduction with albuminuria/urinalysis and cardiovascular risk, then use kidney-protective therapy, medication stewardship and referral for atypical or progressive disease.
recognize: CKD requires persistent kidney abnormality, generally at least 3 months—not one low eGFR during acute illness.
Albuminuria can identify important kidney disease even when eGFR is preserved.
In diabetes, use urine ACR plus eGFR for screening; type 2 diabetes screening begins at diagnosis and repeats yearly.
differentiate: Transient albuminuria can occur with exercise, fever, infection or acute illness; confirm persistence when appropriate.
Hematuria, active sediment, rapid decline, systemic disease or heavy proteinuria may indicate non-diabetic/non-hypertensive kidney disease and need specialist evaluation.
assessment: Assess BP, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, smoking, NSAIDs, volume status, urinary symptoms, family history and medication dosing.
Look for edema, systemic inflammatory signs and complications of advanced CKD.
workup: Use serum creatinine/eGFR and urine ACR; obtain urinalysis/microscopy when CKD is diagnosed or alternative renal disease is suspected.
Trend change over time rather than interpreting eGFR as an exact measurement of kidney function.
management: Optimize BP, diabetes and cardiovascular risk; use kidney-protective RAAS/SGLT2/nsMRA/GLP-1RA therapies where indicated and tolerated.
Avoid nephrotoxins and adjust doses to kidney function.
Refer for rapid progression, significant unexplained proteinuria/hematuria, resistant hypertension, uncertain diagnosis or advanced CKD according to local pathways.
medicationSafety: Avoid NSAIDs in CKD/HTN/HF when safer alternatives exist.
Do not routinely combine ACE inhibitor and ARB.
Monitor potassium/creatinine after RAAS or MRA changes.
counselling: Explain eGFR and albuminuria in plain language; discuss OTC NSAID avoidance and sick-day planning.
Address access to BP/diabetes medications and dietary advice without imposing unnecessary restrictions.
followUp: Monitoring frequency should rise with worse eGFR/albuminuria and faster progression; keep vaccination and cardiovascular prevention current.
examTrap: Calling a single eGFR of 55 during gastroenteritis 'stage 3 CKD' without confirming persistence or checking albuminuria.
oneLinePearl: CKD is chronicity plus eGFR and/or kidney-damage markers—albuminuria matters.

title: UTI, Pyelonephritis, and Asymptomatic Bacteriuria
bottomLine: Treat symptoms, not a positive urine result. Uncomplicated cystitis can often be diagnosed clinically; pyelonephritis is systemic/upper-tract disease; asymptomatic bacteriuria usually should not be screened for or treated except in defined situations such as pregnancy or before selected urologic procedures.
recognize: Cystitis: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort without systemic/upper-tract features.
Pyelonephritis: fever/systemic illness, flank pain/CVA tenderness, nausea/vomiting, with or without lower urinary symptoms.
Older adults commonly have asymptomatic bacteriuria; delirium alone without localizing urinary or systemic infection evidence should not automatically trigger antibiotics.
differentiate: Vaginitis/urethritis/STI can mimic cystitis; vaginal discharge/irritation lowers the probability of isolated bacterial cystitis.
Obstructed infected stone is an emergency, not routine pyelonephritis.
Pregnancy changes thresholds for culture, treatment and follow-up.
assessment: Assess pregnancy, fever, flank pain, vomiting, sepsis features, obstruction/stone history, male anatomy/prostate symptoms, immunocompromise and recurrent infections.
Review recent cultures, antibiotic exposure and local resistance risk.
workup: Urine culture is especially important for pyelonephritis, pregnancy, recurrent/complicated infection or treatment failure.
Do not collect urine cultures from asymptomatic adults without an indication; cloudy/malodorous urine is not diagnostic.
Image when obstruction, stone, abscess or complicated course is suspected—not for routine uncomplicated cystitis.
management: Use local/provincial antimicrobial guidance and previous culture data to select therapy.
Escalate pyelonephritis with sepsis, pregnancy complications, obstruction, inability to tolerate oral intake or unstable comorbidity.
Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in most nonpregnant adults.
medicationSafety: Renally dose antimicrobials where needed and avoid agents unsuitable for suspected tissue/upper-tract infection.
Check pregnancy safety and local resistance patterns before empiric selection.
redFlags: Persistent fever or worsening despite therapy
counselling: Teach hydration to thirst, medication adherence and return precautions for fever/flank pain/vomiting.
Avoid unnecessary repeat cultures in asymptomatic patients after uncomplicated infection unless the clinical context requires them.
followUp: Reassess lack of improvement within the expected timeframe; review culture results and narrow/change therapy when indicated.
examTrap: Treating a positive urinalysis/culture in an older adult with no urinary symptoms and no clear systemic infection source.
oneLinePearl: Bacteria in urine is not the same diagnosis as UTI.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Family Medicine/Geriatrics/Medical Microbiology UTI Recommendations

title: Renal Colic and Hematuria
bottomLine: Most renal colic is painful but stable; the dangerous combination is obstruction plus infection, solitary kidney/bilateral obstruction, uncontrolled symptoms or worsening renal function. Hematuria still requires cause-based follow-up after the acute stone passes.
recognize: Stone pain is typically acute colicky flank pain radiating toward groin with restlessness, nausea and hematuria.
Gross hematuria, persistent microscopic hematuria, older age, smoking history or atypical painless bleeding raises urothelial malignancy concern.
Fever with obstruction is a urologic emergency.
differentiate: AAA, ectopic pregnancy, pyelonephritis, ovarian/testicular torsion and other abdominal emergencies can mimic renal colic.
Absence of hematuria does not exclude a stone.
assessment: Check fever, vitals, hydration, pain control, pregnancy, solitary kidney, prior stones, urinary retention and infection symptoms.
Examine abdomen/flank and evaluate alternate time-sensitive diagnoses.
workup: Urinalysis, pregnancy test when relevant, creatinine and culture if infection suspected.
Select imaging according to age, pregnancy, first episode, diagnostic uncertainty and complication risk; minimize unnecessary radiation.
management: Provide analgesia/antiemetic and hydration to normal needs; do not force excessive fluids during acute obstruction.
Use medical expulsive therapy selectively when evidence/stone characteristics support it.
Emergency urologic decompression is required for infected obstruction; refer based on stone size/location, renal function, persistent obstruction or uncontrolled symptoms.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs are effective for renal colic but may be inappropriate with AKI, CKD, GI bleeding risk or pregnancy considerations.
Opioids may be needed short term when pain is severe but should not replace definitive care for complicated obstruction.
counselling: Discuss stone capture if useful, recurrence prevention after stone type/risk evaluation and explicit emergency signs.
followUp: Confirm symptom/obstruction resolution when indicated and investigate persistent hematuria rather than assuming it was all from the stone.
examTrap: Discharging a febrile patient with an obstructing stone on oral antibiotics alone.
oneLinePearl: Stone plus infection plus obstruction = drainage emergency.
